DeCovarT maximises a Gaussian-convolution log-likelihood for cellular
ratios $\boldsymbol{p}\in\Delta^{J-1}$. This vignette derives the
analytic first- and second-order derivatives used by the frequentist
solvers, first with respect to unconstrained ambient proportions
$\boldsymbol{p}$, then after the isometric log-ratio (ILR) map that
enforces the simplex. It closes with the expected Fisher information and
the ILR delta-method covariance that feed
[`vcov.decovart_fit()`](../reference/fit_decovart.html) and
[`confint.decovart_fit()`](../reference/fit_decovart.html).
Package entry points are
[`gradient_loglik_unconstrained()`](../reference/gradient_loglik_unconstrained.html),
[`hessian_loglik_unconstrained()`](../reference/hessian_loglik_unconstrained.html),
[`gradient_loglik_constrained()`](../reference/gradient_loglik_constrained.html),
[`hessian_loglik_constrained()`](../reference/hessian_loglik_constrained.html),
[`expected_fisher_unconstrained()`](../reference/expected_fisher_unconstrained.html)
and
[`vcov_ilr_delta()`](../reference/vcov_ilr_delta.html).
@sec-constrained compares the softmax, additive, centred and isometric
log-ratio charts and explains why the solvers use ILR.

::: {#nte-notation .callout-note}
## Notation

- Indices: gene $g$; cell types $j,\ell\in\{1,\ldots,J\}$; one bulk
  sample is fixed, so the sample index $i$ is dropped; $a,b$ index ILR
  coordinates.
- $\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}^{G\times J}$: mean signature.
- $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\in\mathrm{SPD}(G)$: cell-type covariance;
  $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})=\sum_j p_j^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$
  and
  $\boldsymbol{\Omega}(\boldsymbol{p})=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})^{-1}$.
- $\boldsymbol{p}$: proportions on the open simplex (ambient score
  equations treat them as free coordinates in $(0,1)^{J}$).
- $\boldsymbol{\rho}\in\mathbb{R}^{J-1}$: unconstrained log-ratio
  coordinates (ILR / Helmert chart $\mathbf{V}$);
  $\boldsymbol{p}=\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\rho})$.
  The manuscript DAG uses the same letter for the ALR chart; here
  $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ denotes the ILR coordinates used by the solvers,
  and $\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\mathrm{alr}}$ the ALR coordinates (@sec-simplex-notation).
:::

# Matrix calculus reminders {#sec-matrix-calculus}

The score and Hessian of the convolution log-likelihood follow from a
handful of matrix-derivative identities. The statements below mirror the
matrix-calculus remarks in the manuscript Methods appendix.

::: {#rem-first-order-matrix}
## First-order matrix calculus

Let $\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{A}(p)$ and $\boldsymbol{B}=\boldsymbol{B}(p)$
be invertible matrix-valued functions of a scalar $p$, and let
$\boldsymbol{U}$, $\boldsymbol{V}$ be constant matrices of compatible size.
Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial\det(\boldsymbol{A})}{\partial p}
&=
\det(\boldsymbol{A})\,
\mathrm{tr}\!\left(
  \boldsymbol{A}^{-1}
  \frac{\partial\boldsymbol{A}}{\partial p}
\right),
\\
\frac{\partial(\boldsymbol{U}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{V})}{\partial p}
&=
\boldsymbol{U}
\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{A}}{\partial p}
\boldsymbol{V},
\\
\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}}{\partial p}
&=
-
\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}
\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{A}}{\partial p}
\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-matrix-first-order}

The chain rule on $\log\det$ yields

$$
\frac{\partial\log\det(\boldsymbol{A})}{\partial p}
=
\mathrm{tr}\!\left(
  \boldsymbol{A}^{-1}
  \frac{\partial\boldsymbol{A}}{\partial p}
\right),
\qquad
\frac{\partial\log\det(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1})}{\partial p}
=
-
\mathrm{tr}\!\left(
  \boldsymbol{A}^{-1}
  \frac{\partial\boldsymbol{A}}{\partial p}
\right).
$$ {#eq-logdet}

For a residual quadratic form with symmetric precision
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ and mean map linear in $p$,

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial p}
\bigl(
  (\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{x}p)^{\top}
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}
  (\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{x}p)
\bigr)
=
-2\,
\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{x}p).
$$ {#eq-quad-form-deriv}
:::

::: {#rem-second-order-matrix}
## Second-order matrix calculus

Differentiating the inverse once more gives

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}}{\partial p_{j}\partial p_{\ell}}
=
\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}
\Biggl(
  \frac{\partial\boldsymbol{A}}{\partial p_{j}}
  \boldsymbol{A}^{-1}
  \frac{\partial\boldsymbol{A}}{\partial p_{\ell}}
  -
  \frac{\partial^{2}\boldsymbol{A}}{\partial p_{j}\partial p_{\ell}}
  +
  \frac{\partial\boldsymbol{A}}{\partial p_{\ell}}
  \boldsymbol{A}^{-1}
  \frac{\partial\boldsymbol{A}}{\partial p_{j}}
\Biggr)
\boldsymbol{A}^{-1},
$$ {#eq-matrix-second-order}

and the trace is linear,
$\partial\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol{A})/\partial p_{j}
=\mathrm{tr}(\partial\boldsymbol{A}/\partial p_{j})$. Combining
@eq-matrix-first-order with that linearity yields

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}\log\det(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1})}{\partial p_{j}\partial p_{\ell}}
=
-
\mathrm{tr}\!\left[
  \boldsymbol{A}^{-1}
  \frac{\partial^{2}\boldsymbol{A}}{\partial p_{j}\partial p_{\ell}}
\right]
+
\mathrm{tr}\!\left[
  \left(
    \boldsymbol{A}^{-1}
    \frac{\partial\boldsymbol{A}}{\partial p_{j}}
  \right)
  \left(
    \boldsymbol{A}^{-1}
    \frac{\partial\boldsymbol{A}}{\partial p_{\ell}}
  \right)
\right].
$$ {#eq-logdet-hess}
:::

::: {#nte-inner-products .callout-tip}
## Inner products in the score

Several terms are $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$-inner products of signature
columns,
$\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot \ell}$.
Package helper [`.inner_product()`](../reference/dot-inner_product.html)
evaluates that bilinear form; see also the squared Mahalanobis distance
helper in the same family.
:::

# Unconstrained score and Hessian {#sec-unconstrained}

Conditional on the reference moments
$\boldsymbol{\zeta}=(\boldsymbol{\mu},\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}\})$, the
bulk follows
$\boldsymbol{y}\mid\boldsymbol{\zeta},\boldsymbol{p}
\sim\mathcal{N}_{G}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p},
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})\bigr)$. Up to an additive constant
independent of $\boldsymbol{p}$,

$$
\ell_{\boldsymbol{y}\mid\boldsymbol{\zeta}}(\boldsymbol{p})
=
\tfrac{1}{2}\log\det\boldsymbol{\Omega}(\boldsymbol{p})
-
\tfrac{1}{2}
(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})^{\top}
\boldsymbol{\Omega}(\boldsymbol{p})
(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}).
$$ {#eq-loglik}

::: {#nte-halfdet .callout-important}
## The determinant term carries a factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$

Both terms of @eq-loglik are halved, because
$\log\det\boldsymbol{\Omega}=-\log\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ enters the
Gaussian log-density as
$-\tfrac{1}{2}\log\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})$. DeCovarT
releases before 2.3.0 implemented
$-\log\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})$, which doubled the
determinant contribution. The objective was then *not* the stated
Gaussian model, and it disagreed with the expected Fisher information of
@sec-fisher-wald, which had always been the one implied by the correct
density. With the factor restored,
`loglik_multivariate()` matches `mvtnorm::dmvnorm(..., log = TRUE)` up to
the constant $\tfrac{G}{2}\log(2\pi)$, and
$\mathbb{E}[-\mathbf{H}]=I(\boldsymbol{p})$ holds exactly
(see @nte-obs-vs-exp). Point estimates move only slightly, because the
two terms trade off differently, but likelihood **values**, AIC,
likelihood-ratio statistics, and any curvature-based standard error do
change.
:::

::: {#nte-unconstrained-meaning .callout-warning}
## What “unconstrained” means here

@sec-unconstrained treats each $p_{j}$ as an ambient coordinate in
$(0,1)$ and ignores $\sum_{j}p_{j}=1$. The resulting gradient and
Hessian are the building blocks of the ILR chain rule in
@sec-constrained. They are **not** the coordinates used by
Marquardt–Levenberg or Newton–Raphson in the package (those optimise in
$\boldsymbol{\rho}$-space). The box-constrained L-BFGS-B path is the
exception: it works directly in $\boldsymbol{p}$ with $[0,1]^{J}$ boxes
and does not enforce the simplex exactly.
:::

Applying @eq-logdet and @eq-quad-form-deriv with
$\partial\boldsymbol{\Sigma}/\partial p_{j}=2p_{j}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}$
gives the ambient score.

::: {#thm-score-unconstrained}
## Unconstrained gradient

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial p_{j}}
&=
\underbrace{-p_{j}\,\mathrm{tr}\bigl(
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}
\bigr)}_{\text{purple}}
+
\underbrace{
  (\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})^{\top}
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}
  \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}
}_{\text{blue}}
\\
&\quad+
\underbrace{
  p_{j}\,
  (\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})^{\top}
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}
  \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}
  (\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})
}_{\text{orange}}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-grad-unconstrained}
:::

Differentiating @eq-grad-unconstrained once more yields the ambient
Hessian $\mathbf{H}\in\mathcal{M}_{J\times J}$. Diagonal and off-diagonal
blocks keep the same colour pairing.

::: {#thm-hess-unconstrained}
## Unconstrained Hessian

For $j\in\{1,\ldots,J\}$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{H}_{jj}
&=
\frac{\partial^{2}\ell}{\partial p_{j}^{2}}
=
\underbrace{
  -\,\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j})
  +
  2p_{j}^{2}\,\mathrm{tr}\bigl(
    (\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j})^{2}
  \bigr)
}_{\text{purple}}
\\
&\quad
\underbrace{
  -2p_{j}
  (\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})^{\top}
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}
  \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}
  \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}
  -
  \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}^{\top}
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}
  \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}
}_{\text{blue}}
\\
&\quad
\underbrace{
  -2p_{j}
  (\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})^{\top}
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}
  \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}
  \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}
  -
  (\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})^{\top}
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}
  \bigl(
    4p_{j}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}
    -
    \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}
  \bigr)
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}
  (\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})
}_{\text{orange}},
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-hess-diag}

and for $j\neq\ell$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{H}_{j\ell}
&=
\frac{\partial^{2}\ell}{\partial p_{j}\partial p_{\ell}}
=
\underbrace{
  2p_{j}p_{\ell}\,
  \mathrm{tr}\bigl(
    \boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell}
    \boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}
  \bigr)
}_{\text{purple}}
\\
&\quad
\underbrace{
  -2p_{j}
  (\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})^{\top}
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}
  \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}
  \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot \ell}
  -
  \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}^{\top}
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}
  \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot \ell}
}_{\text{blue}}
\\
&\quad
\underbrace{
  -2p_{\ell}
  (\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})^{\top}
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}
  \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell}
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}
  \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}
  -
  4p_{j}p_{\ell}
  (\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})^{\top}
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}
  \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}
  \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell}
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}
  (\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})
}_{\text{orange}}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-hess-off}
:::

The stationary equation $\nabla\ell(\boldsymbol{p})=\boldsymbol{0}$ has
no closed root, so DeCovarT uses iterative solvers. Analytic gradients
and Hessians are checked against Richardson extrapolation in
`numDeriv` [@R-numDeriv].

# Constrained optimisation on the simplex {#sec-constrained}

The cellular ratios satisfy $p_{j}\ge 0$ and $\sum_{j}p_{j}=1$, the
*compositional* or unit-simplex constraint. An optimiser can handle it in
three ways: eliminate it with a reparametrisation, enforce it softly with
penalties or barriers, or enforce it exactly with projections and
Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) conditions. DeCovarT uses the first route: a
$C^{2}$ diffeomorphism from free Euclidean coordinates onto the open
simplex, so every Newton step stays feasible by construction. Four such
charts are common: the softmax, the additive log-ratio (ALR), the centred
log-ratio (CLR) and the isometric log-ratio (ILR). This section defines
the notation they share (@sec-simplex-notation), presents each chart
(@sec-lse--@sec-ilr), explains why DeCovarT uses ILR (@sec-chart-choice)
and compares the four side by side (@sec-chart-comparison). The
derivatives of the ILR chart (@sec-ilr-deriv, @sec-chain-rule), their
link to the Lagrangian (@sec-kkt) and perspectives on Bayesian charts
and exact zeros (@sec-structural-zeros) follow.

The compositional background is chapter 4 of
*Modelling and Analysis of Compositional Data*
[@CoordinateRepresentation2015], cited below by page.

## Notation for compositions and charts {#sec-simplex-notation}

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| $\Delta^{J-1}=\{\boldsymbol{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{J}:p_{j}\ge 0,\ \mathbf{1}_{J}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{p}=1\}$ | closed unit simplex of $J$ cell types; its interior $\mathring{\Delta}^{J-1}$ has $p_{j}>0$ for all $j$ |
| $\mathbf{1}_{J}$, $\mathbf{I}_{J}$ | vector of ones, identity matrix |
| $\mathbf{H}_{J}=\mathbf{I}_{J}-\tfrac{1}{J}\mathbf{1}_{J}\mathbf{1}_{J}^{\mathsf{T}}$ | centring matrix: orthogonal projector onto $\mathbf{1}_{J}^{\perp}=\{\boldsymbol{w}:\mathbf{1}_{J}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{w}=0\}$ |
| $\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{x}/(\mathbf{1}_{J}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{x})$ | closure of a positive vector $\boldsymbol{x}\in(0,\infty)^{J}$ |
| $\log\boldsymbol{p}$, $\exp\boldsymbol{z}$ | applied component by component |
| $g(\boldsymbol{p})=\bigl(\prod_{j}p_{j}\bigr)^{1/J}$ | geometric mean |
| $\operatorname{softmax}(\boldsymbol{z})=\mathcal{C}(\exp\boldsymbol{z})$ | closure of exponentiated scores $\boldsymbol{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{J}$ |
| $\boldsymbol{\psi}$ | a chart: a smooth bijection from free coordinates onto $\mathring{\Delta}^{J-1}$ |
| $\boldsymbol{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{J}$, $\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\mathrm{alr}}\in\mathbb{R}^{J-1}$, $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathbf{1}_{J}^{\perp}$, $\boldsymbol{\rho}\in\mathbb{R}^{J-1}$ | softmax scores, ALR coordinates (reference $J$ unless a superscript names it), CLR and ILR coordinates |
| $\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{J\times(J-1)}$ | Helmert basis of the ILR chart (@sec-helmert) |
| $\mathbf{D}_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{(J-1)\times J}$ | ALR contrast with reference $r$: rows $\boldsymbol{e}_{j}^{\mathsf{T}}-\boldsymbol{e}_{r}^{\mathsf{T}}$, $j\neq r$ |
| $\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{p})-\boldsymbol{p}\boldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}}$ | Jacobian of the softmax at $\boldsymbol{p}$ |

: Notation for compositions and their charts. {#tbl-simplex-notation}

**The closure operator.** $\mathcal{C}$ rescales any positive vector to
unit sum. It discards the total and keeps the relative sizes:
$\mathcal{C}(c\boldsymbol{x})=\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{x})$ for every
$c>0$. A composition is therefore an equivalence class of proportional
positive vectors, and $\mathcal{C}$ picks its representative on the
simplex [@CoordinateRepresentation2015, pp. 33--35]. Two consequences
matter here.

- Only scale-free functions of $\boldsymbol{p}$ are meaningful, and the
  log-ratios $\log(p_{j}/p_{\ell})$ are the simplest. A constant added to
  $\log\boldsymbol{p}$ does not change the composition, so every
  log-ratio chart must cancel the direction $\mathbf{1}_{J}$.
- Closure creates dependence. Library-size normalisation of counts is a
  closure, and it induces negative covariances between parts that need
  not exist in the absolute abundances.

Closure also gives the simplex a Euclidean vector-space structure, the
*Aitchison geometry*: perturbation
$\boldsymbol{x}\oplus\boldsymbol{y}=\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{x}\circ\boldsymbol{y})$
plays the role of addition, powering
$\alpha\odot\boldsymbol{x}=\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{x}^{\alpha})$ the role
of scalar multiplication, and the inner product is
$\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\rangle_{a}
=\operatorname{clr}(\boldsymbol{x})^{\mathsf{T}}\operatorname{clr}(\boldsymbol{y})$
[@CoordinateRepresentation2015, Property 4.2, p. 35]. The log-ratio charts
below are linear maps for this structure; they differ in whether they
also preserve its inner product.

## Softmax and log-sum-exp {#sec-lse}

The softmax of scores $\boldsymbol{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{J}$ is evaluated
through the log-sum-exp (LSE) to avoid overflow,

$$
s_{j}
=
\frac{e^{z_{j}}}{\sum_{\ell}e^{z_{\ell}}}
=
e^{z_{j}-\operatorname{LSE}(\boldsymbol{z})},
\qquad
\operatorname{LSE}(\boldsymbol{z})
=
z_{\max}+\log\sum_{\ell}e^{z_{\ell}-z_{\max}},
\quad
z_{\max}=\max_{\ell}z_{\ell}.
$$ {#eq-softmax}

Its Jacobian is
$\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{softmax}}=\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{s})
=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{s})-\boldsymbol{s}\boldsymbol{s}^{\mathsf{T}}$,
which is also $\nabla^{2}\operatorname{LSE}(\boldsymbol{z})$. The second
derivative is the third-order tensor

$$
H_{j\ell m}
=
s_{j}\bigl[
  (\delta_{j\ell}-s_{\ell})(\delta_{jm}-s_{m})
  -
  s_{\ell}(\delta_{\ell m}-s_{m})
\bigr].
$$ {#eq-softmax-hess}

The softmax with $J$ free scores is over-parametrised:
$\operatorname{softmax}(\boldsymbol{z}+c\mathbf{1}_{J})
=\operatorname{softmax}(\boldsymbol{z})$, because closure removes the
common factor $e^{c}$. Accordingly $\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{s})\mathbf{1}_{J}=\boldsymbol{0}$,
the Jacobian has rank $J-1$, and the Hessian of
$\ell(\operatorname{softmax}(\boldsymbol{z}))$ has a zero eigenvalue along
$\mathbf{1}_{J}$: a Newton system in $\boldsymbol{z}$ is singular. The
three log-ratio charts are three ways to remove this redundant
direction. Each writes
$\boldsymbol{p}=\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{\theta})$
with $\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{J-1}$ and a matrix
$\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{J\times(J-1)}$ whose columns, together with
$\mathbf{1}_{J}$, span $\mathbb{R}^{J}$. ALR pins one score to zero, CLR
constrains the scores to sum to zero, and ILR spans $\mathbf{1}_{J}^{\perp}$
with an orthonormal basis.

## Additive log-ratio chart {#sec-alr}

Pin a reference cell type $r$, by default the last one ($r=J$). The ALR
coordinates and their inverse, the *additive logistic* transform, are
[@aitchisonStatisticalAnalysisCompositional1982]

$$
\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{j}
=
\log\!\left(\frac{p_{j}}{p_{J}}\right),
\qquad
p_{j}
=
\frac{e^{\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{j}}}{1+\sum_{\ell<J}e^{\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{\ell}}}\ (j<J),
\qquad
p_{J}
=
\frac{1}{1+\sum_{\ell<J}e^{\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{\ell}}}.
$$ {#eq-alr-maps}

Equivalently
$\boldsymbol{p}=\operatorname{softmax}(\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{1},\ldots,\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{J-1},0)$
and $\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\mathrm{alr}}=\mathbf{D}_{J}\log\boldsymbol{p}$. The "1" in the
denominator is the reference part; the word *additive* refers to the
sum of exponentials in that denominator, not to the Aitchison
perturbation [@CoordinateRepresentation2015, p. 47]. The package
solvers use the isometric chart below, not this additive one. The
Jacobian of @eq-alr-maps is the softmax Jacobian with the reference
column dropped,
$\partial p_{j}/\partial\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{a}=p_{j}(\delta_{ja}-p_{a})$ for
$a=1,\ldots,J-1$.

::: {#exm-alr-numeric}
## ALR in both directions for $\boldsymbol{p}=(0.5,0.3,0.2)$

Colours track each cell type: $\textcolor{#1d4e89}{p_{1}}$,
$\textcolor{#c45c26}{p_{2}}$ and the reference
$\textcolor{#7b3294}{p_{3}}$.

*Forward.* Each coordinate compares one cell type with the reference,
so the reference enters both coordinates:

$$
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{1}
&=\log\frac{\textcolor{#1d4e89}{p_{1}}}{\textcolor{#7b3294}{p_{3}}}
=\log\frac{\textcolor{#1d4e89}{0.5}}{\textcolor{#7b3294}{0.2}}
=\log 2.5\approx 0.916\\
\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{2}
&=\log\frac{\textcolor{#c45c26}{p_{2}}}{\textcolor{#7b3294}{p_{3}}}
=\log\frac{\textcolor{#c45c26}{0.3}}{\textcolor{#7b3294}{0.2}}
=\log 1.5\approx 0.405
\end{aligned}
\right.
$$

*Backward.* Exponentiate each coordinate, give the reference the weight
$e^{0}=1$, then close; the common denominator is
$1+e^{\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{1}}+e^{\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{2}}=1+2.5+1.5=5$:

$$
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
\textcolor{#1d4e89}{p_{1}}
&=\frac{e^{\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{1}}}{1+e^{\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{1}}+e^{\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{2}}}
=\frac{\textcolor{#1d4e89}{2.5}}{5}
=\textcolor{#1d4e89}{0.5}\\
\textcolor{#c45c26}{p_{2}}
&=\frac{e^{\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{2}}}{1+e^{\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{1}}+e^{\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{2}}}
=\frac{\textcolor{#c45c26}{1.5}}{5}
=\textcolor{#c45c26}{0.3}\\
\textcolor{#7b3294}{p_{3}}
&=\frac{1}{1+e^{\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{1}}+e^{\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{2}}}
=\frac{\textcolor{#7b3294}{1}}{5}
=\textcolor{#7b3294}{0.2}
\end{aligned}
\right.
$$

*Changing the reference.* With $\textcolor{#1d4e89}{p_{1}}$ as reference
(superscript $1$),
$\rho^{\mathrm{alr},1}_{1}=\log(\textcolor{#c45c26}{p_{2}}/\textcolor{#1d4e89}{p_{1}})\approx-0.511$
and
$\rho^{\mathrm{alr},1}_{2}=\log(\textcolor{#7b3294}{p_{3}}/\textcolor{#1d4e89}{p_{1}})\approx-0.916$,
that is $\rho^{\mathrm{alr},1}_{1}=\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{2}-\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{1}$ and $\rho^{\mathrm{alr},1}_{2}=-\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{1}$. The
two charts are related by the matrix
$\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, which is
invertible but not orthogonal: its singular values are $1.618$ and
$0.618$, so it stretches some directions $2.6$ times more than others.
:::

**What the reference changes, and what it does not.** All ALR charts
describe the same family of compositions; only the coordinates differ.
@sec-chart-choice shows that the estimate $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$, the
maximised log-likelihood and the delta-method covariance of
$\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$ do not depend on the reference. The numerical
geometry does: ALR coordinates refer to an oblique, non-orthogonal basis
of the simplex [@CoordinateRepresentation2015, p. 47], so Euclidean
lengths, angles and Hessian condition numbers in $\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\mathrm{alr}}$
change with the reference.

## Centred log-ratio coefficients {#sec-clr}

The CLR transform divides each part by the geometric mean
[@aitchisonStatisticalAnalysisCompositional1982]:

$$
\boldsymbol{\xi}
=
\operatorname{clr}(\boldsymbol{p})
=
\log\frac{\boldsymbol{p}}{g(\boldsymbol{p})}
=
\mathbf{H}_{J}\log\boldsymbol{p},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{p}
=
\mathcal{C}(\exp\boldsymbol{\xi})
=
\operatorname{softmax}(\boldsymbol{\xi}).
$$ {#eq-clr-maps}

CLR treats every cell type symmetrically and preserves the Aitchison
geometry: distances and inner products between compositions equal
Euclidean ones between their CLR vectors
[@CoordinateRepresentation2015, Property 4.2, p. 35]. Pairwise log-ratios are differences,
$\log(p_{j}/p_{\ell})=\xi_{j}-\xi_{\ell}$. The price is a constraint on the
coefficients: $\mathbf{1}_{J}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\xi}=0$. CLR gives
$J$ coefficients for $J-1$ degrees of freedom, so they are not
coordinates in a basis, a random CLR vector has a singular covariance
matrix, and the coefficients change when a subcomposition is analysed
[@CoordinateRepresentation2015, pp. 34--35]. Optimising over a free
$\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^{J}$ is the over-parametrised softmax of
@sec-lse again.

CLR is nevertheless the hub between the other charts. Since
$\mathbf{D}_{r}\mathbf{1}_{J}=\boldsymbol{0}$ and
$\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{1}_{J}=\boldsymbol{0}$, both ALR and ILR
are linear images of CLR:
$\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\mathrm{alr}}=\mathbf{D}_{r}\boldsymbol{\xi}$ and
$\boldsymbol{\rho}=\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\xi}$.

## Isometric log-ratio chart {#sec-ilr}

ILR expresses $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ in an orthonormal basis of the
hyperplane $\mathbf{1}_{J}^{\perp}$
[@egozcueIsometricLogratioTransformations2003]. Choose
$\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{J\times(J-1)}$ with

$$
\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{I}_{J-1},
\qquad
\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{1}_{J}=\mathbf{0},
\qquad
\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}=\mathbf{H}_{J}.
$$ {#eq-helmert}

ILR coordinates and their inverse are
[@pawlowsky-glahnCompositionalDataAnalysis2011]

$$
\boldsymbol{\rho}
=
\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\log\boldsymbol{p}
=
\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\operatorname{clr}(\boldsymbol{p}),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{p}
=
\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\rho})
=
\mathcal{C}\bigl\{\exp(\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\rho})\bigr\}.
$$ {#eq-ilr-maps}

In the book's notation the contrast matrix is
$\boldsymbol{\Psi}=\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}$, and @eq-helmert is its
Eq. (4.5); @eq-ilr-maps is Eqs. (4.7)--(4.8)
[@CoordinateRepresentation2015, pp. 36--37]. ILR keeps the strengths of both previous charts: like
ALR it gives $J-1$ unconstrained coordinates, and like CLR it preserves
the Aitchison geometry, now with
$d_{a}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})
=\lVert\operatorname{ilr}(\boldsymbol{x})-\operatorname{ilr}(\boldsymbol{y})\rVert$
(Property 4.5, p. 37). No cell type is a reference. Package helpers
[`helmert_basis()`](../reference/helmert_basis.html),
[`isometric_logistic()`](../reference/isometric_logistic.html) and
[`isometric_log_ratio()`](../reference/isometric_log_ratio.html)
implement @eq-helmert--@eq-ilr-maps with a log-sum-exp softmax, matching
the `compositions::ilr()` / `ilrInv()` convention on a Helmert basis
[@R-compositions].

### The Helmert basis: definition, role and use {#sec-helmert}

**Definition.** The ILR chart needs one orthonormal basis of
$\mathbf{1}_{J}^{\perp}$; there are infinitely many. The Helmert basis
is the one with a closed form. Column $k=1,\ldots,J-1$ of
[`helmert_basis()`](../reference/helmert_basis.html) is

$$
\boldsymbol{v}_{k}
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{k(k+1)}}
\bigl(\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{k},\,-k,\,\underbrace{0,\ldots,0}_{J-k-1}\bigr)^{\mathsf{T}}.
$$ {#eq-helmert-columns}

Each column sums to zero and has unit norm, and two columns are
orthogonal because the later one is constant on the support of the
earlier one. The basis is the Gram--Schmidt orthonormalisation of the
generating system of the simplex
[@egozcueIsometricLogratioTransformations2003], and its contrast matrix
is a Helmert matrix without the constant row
[@CoordinateRepresentation2015, Example 4.6, p. 40]. The book lists the same basis in reverse
order, with the first coordinate contrasting the first $J-1$ parts with
the last one.

**Role: every coordinate is a balance.** Inserting
@eq-helmert-columns into @eq-ilr-maps gives

$$
\rho_{k}
=
\boldsymbol{v}_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\log\boldsymbol{p}
=
\sqrt{\frac{k}{k+1}}\,
\log\frac{g(p_{1},\ldots,p_{k})}{p_{k+1}},
$$ {#eq-helmert-balance}

the normalised log-ratio between the geometric mean of the first $k$
cell types and type $k+1$. This is the *balance* of a sequential binary
partition: level $k$ splits $\{1,\ldots,k+1\}$ into $\{1,\ldots,k\}$
(sign $+$) and $\{k+1\}$ (sign $-$)
[@CoordinateRepresentation2015, Eq. (4.9), pp. 38--39]. For $J=4$ the sign matrix is

| Level | $p_{1}$ | $p_{2}$ | $p_{3}$ | $p_{4}$ |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| $\rho_{1}$ | $+$ | $-$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| $\rho_{2}$ | $+$ | $+$ | $-$ | $0$ |
| $\rho_{3}$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ | $-$ |

: Sequential binary partition encoded by the Helmert basis for $J=4$. {#tbl-helmert-sbp}

The factor $\sqrt{k/(k+1)}$ makes balances comparable across levels.
Balances are geometrically orthogonal, so each carries information the
others do not; geometric orthogonality does not imply that their
estimates are uncorrelated [@CoordinateRepresentation2015, p. 41].
The Helmert basis thus does three jobs at once:

- it cancels the closure direction, because every column sums to zero:
  adding a constant to $\log\boldsymbol{p}$ leaves $\boldsymbol{\rho}$
  unchanged;
- it removes the redundant softmax direction while keeping Euclidean
  geometry, because the columns are orthonormal;
- it is explicit and sparse, so $\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\rho}$ costs
  $O(J)$ operations per column and needs no QR or Gram--Schmidt step at
  run time.

**Use in practice.** DeCovarT builds $\mathbf{V}$ once from $J$ and
proceeds as follows.

1. Map a starting composition to coordinates with
   `isometric_log_ratio(p)`, which computes $\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\log\boldsymbol{p}$.
2. Iterate on $\boldsymbol{\rho}\in\mathbb{R}^{J-1}$ with the score and
   Hessian of @thm-chain-rule; no step can leave the simplex.
3. Map back with `isometric_logistic(rho)`, a log-sum-exp softmax of
   $\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\rho}$.
4. Push the covariance of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ to
   $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$ with the Jacobian $\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})\mathbf{V}$
   (@sec-fisher-rho).

The order of the cell types fixes which balances are reported, not the
estimate. Both helpers accept another basis through their `V` argument:
for instance, a partition that first contrasts immune with stromal
types gives coordinates with a biological reading. Any such basis is
$\mathbf{V}Q$ for an orthogonal $Q$ (@prp-ilr-rotation).

![The ILR chart is an isometry from the simplex to Euclidean space.
**A** ($J=2$): the simplex is a segment and the ILR chart a line;
equally spaced values of $\rho$ (colour) map to compositions that crowd
towards the vertices. **B** ($J=3$): lines of constant $\rho_{1}$ (solid)
and $\rho_{2}$ (dotted) on the ternary triangle, the composition
$(0.5,0.3,0.2)$ and two segments of Aitchison length 1, one near the
barycentre (green) and one near the vertex $p_{3}=1$ (gold). **C**: the
same objects in ILR coordinates, where the grid is orthonormal and both
segments have Euclidean length 1. **D**: in the plane orthogonal to
$\mathbf{1}_{3}$, Gram--Schmidt applied to $\boldsymbol{a}_{1}=\boldsymbol{e}_{1}-\boldsymbol{e}_{2}$
and $\boldsymbol{a}_{2}=\boldsymbol{e}_{2}-\boldsymbol{e}_{3}$ normalises
$\boldsymbol{a}_{1}$ into $\boldsymbol{v}_{1}$, removes from
$\boldsymbol{a}_{2}$ its projection on $\boldsymbol{v}_{1}$ (orange), and
normalises the residual into $\boldsymbol{v}_{2}$: the two Helmert columns
of @eq-helmert-columns. Dashed lines are the CLR images of the canonical
vectors. Script: `scripts/auxiliary/generate_ilr_isometry_figure.R`.](figures/ilr_isometry_gram_schmidt.png){#fig-ilr-isometry width=100%}

@fig-ilr-isometry summarises the construction. Gram--Schmidt applied to
the successive differences $\boldsymbol{e}_{k}-\boldsymbol{e}_{k+1}$,
which span $\mathbf{1}_{J}^{\perp}$, returns exactly the columns of
@eq-helmert-columns for every $J$ (panel D); the resulting chart is
isometric, so equal Aitchison lengths become equal Euclidean lengths
(panels B--C).

::: {#exm-ilr-numeric}
## ILR in both directions for $\boldsymbol{p}=(0.5,0.3,0.2)$

For $J=3$ the Helmert columns are
$\boldsymbol{v}_{1}=(1,-1,0)^{\mathsf{T}}/\sqrt{2}$ and
$\boldsymbol{v}_{2}=(1,1,-2)^{\mathsf{T}}/\sqrt{6}$. The entries of
$\mathbf{V}$ are the weights each coordinate gives to each
$\log\textcolor{#1d4e89}{p_{1}}$, $\log\textcolor{#c45c26}{p_{2}}$ and
$\log\textcolor{#7b3294}{p_{3}}$; in each coordinate the weights sum to zero.

*Forward*, $\boldsymbol{\rho}=\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\log\boldsymbol{p}$:

$$
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
\rho_{1}
&=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\log\textcolor{#1d4e89}{p_{1}}
 -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\log\textcolor{#c45c26}{p_{2}}
 +0\cdot\log\textcolor{#7b3294}{p_{3}}
 =\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\log\frac{\textcolor{#1d4e89}{0.5}}{\textcolor{#c45c26}{0.3}}
 \approx 0.361\\
\rho_{2}
&=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\log\textcolor{#1d4e89}{p_{1}}
 +\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\log\textcolor{#c45c26}{p_{2}}
 -\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\log\textcolor{#7b3294}{p_{3}}
 =\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{3}}\log\frac{\sqrt{\textcolor{#1d4e89}{0.5}\times\textcolor{#c45c26}{0.3}}}{\textcolor{#7b3294}{0.2}}
 \approx 0.540
\end{aligned}
\right.
$$

$\rho_{1}$ balances type 1 against type 2; $\rho_{2}$ balances their
geometric mean against type 3.

*Backward*, in two steps. First $\boldsymbol{\xi}=\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\rho}$,
read row by row, so row $j$ of $\mathbf{V}$ rebuilds the CLR
coefficient of cell type $j$:

$$
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
\textcolor{#1d4e89}{\xi_{1}}
&=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\rho_{1}+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\rho_{2}
\approx 0.255+0.220=0.476\\
\textcolor{#c45c26}{\xi_{2}}
&=-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\rho_{1}+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\rho_{2}
\approx -0.255+0.220=-0.035\\
\textcolor{#7b3294}{\xi_{3}}
&=0\cdot\rho_{1}-\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\rho_{2}
\approx -0.441
\end{aligned}
\right.
$$

Then exponentiate and close; the common denominator is
$e^{\xi_{1}}+e^{\xi_{2}}+e^{\xi_{3}}\approx 1.609+0.966+0.644=3.218$:

$$
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
\textcolor{#1d4e89}{p_{1}}
&=\frac{e^{\xi_{1}}}{e^{\xi_{1}}+e^{\xi_{2}}+e^{\xi_{3}}}
\approx\frac{\textcolor{#1d4e89}{1.609}}{3.218}
=\textcolor{#1d4e89}{0.5}\\
\textcolor{#c45c26}{p_{2}}
&=\frac{e^{\xi_{2}}}{e^{\xi_{1}}+e^{\xi_{2}}+e^{\xi_{3}}}
\approx\frac{\textcolor{#c45c26}{0.966}}{3.218}
=\textcolor{#c45c26}{0.3}\\
\textcolor{#7b3294}{p_{3}}
&=\frac{e^{\xi_{3}}}{e^{\xi_{1}}+e^{\xi_{2}}+e^{\xi_{3}}}
\approx\frac{\textcolor{#7b3294}{0.644}}{3.218}
=\textcolor{#7b3294}{0.2}
\end{aligned}
\right.
$$

The intermediate $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ is exactly
$\operatorname{clr}(\boldsymbol{p})$.

*Link with ALR.* Since $\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{j}=\xi_{j}-\xi_{3}$,

$$
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{1}&=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\rho_{1}+\tfrac{3}{\sqrt{6}}\rho_{2}\approx 0.255+0.661=0.916\\
\rho^{\mathrm{alr}}_{2}&=-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\rho_{1}+\tfrac{3}{\sqrt{6}}\rho_{2}\approx -0.255+0.661=0.405
\end{aligned}
\right.
$$

which recovers @exm-alr-numeric. The matrix
$\mathbf{A}_{3}=\mathbf{D}_{3}\mathbf{V}$ of this map has orthogonal
columns of lengths $1$ and $\sqrt{3}$: ALR keeps $\rho_{1}$ at unit
scale and stretches $\rho_{2}$, the balance of the reference
$\textcolor{#7b3294}{p_{3}}$ against the rest, by $\sqrt{3}$.
:::

::: {#prp-ilr-diffeo}
## ILR is a $C^{2}$ diffeomorphism

$\boldsymbol{\psi}:\mathbb{R}^{J-1}\to\mathring{\Delta}^{J-1}$,
$\boldsymbol{\rho}\mapsto\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\rho})$,
is bijective and infinitely differentiable, with inverse
$\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\log\boldsymbol{p}$. Every critical point in
$\boldsymbol{\rho}$-space maps to a unique composition in the open
simplex, and conversely.
:::

## Why DeCovarT uses the ILR chart {#sec-chart-choice}

The question is which chart to optimise in, given that all of them
describe the same model. Two kinds of invariance answer it: statistical
invariance, which every chart has, and numerical invariance, which only
ILR has under a change of convention.

**Statistical invariance holds for every chart.** Let
$\boldsymbol{\theta}'=\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\theta}$ be any invertible
linear change of coordinates, for instance between ILR and ALR
($\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\mathrm{alr}}=\mathbf{A}_{r}\boldsymbol{\rho}$ with
$\mathbf{A}_{r}=\mathbf{D}_{r}\mathbf{V}$) or between two ALR
references. The likelihood is a function of $\boldsymbol{p}$ alone, so
the maximiser is equivariant and $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$ and
$\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}})$ are the same in every chart. The delta
method is invariant too: the Jacobian becomes
$\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}\mathbf{A}^{-1}$ and the information
$\mathbf{A}^{-\mathsf{T}}\mathcal{I}\mathbf{A}^{-1}$, so

$$
\bigl(\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}\mathbf{A}^{-1}\bigr)
\bigl(\mathbf{A}^{-\mathsf{T}}\mathcal{I}\mathbf{A}^{-1}\bigr)^{-1}
\bigl(\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}\mathbf{A}^{-1}\bigr)^{\mathsf{T}}
=
\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}\mathcal{I}^{-1}\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}^{\mathsf{T}}.
$$ {#eq-delta-invariance}

In this sense ALR is reference-invariant: whichever cell type is the
denominator, a correct implementation returns the same
$\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$ and the same Wald covariance for
$\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$. A material change in $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$ when
the reference is permuted signals a numerical or convergence problem,
not a statistical dependence on the reference. Pure Newton steps share
this invariance, because the Newton step is invariant under affine
changes of coordinates [@boydConvexOptimization2004, sec. 9.5].

**Numerical invariance differs.** What changes with the chart is the
Euclidean geometry the solver sees: gradient norms, damping, stopping
rules and the condition number of the Hessian, which controls the
floating-point accuracy of every linear solve and of
$\mathcal{I}^{-1}$.

::: {#prp-ilr-rotation}
## Conditioning under a change of chart

(i) *ILR.* Any two orthonormal bases of $\mathbf{1}_{J}^{\perp}$ satisfy
$\mathbf{V}^{\star}=\mathbf{V}Q$ with $Q^{\mathsf{T}}Q=\mathbf{I}_{J-1}$.
Then $\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\star}=Q^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\rho}$,
$\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\star}}\ell=Q^{\mathsf{T}}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}\ell$
and
$\mathbf{H}_{\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\star}}=Q^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{H}_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}Q$.
Gradient norms, Hessian eigenvalues and condition numbers are identical
in every orthonormal basis.

(ii) *ALR.* For every reference $r$, $\mathbf{A}_{r}=\mathbf{D}_{r}\mathbf{V}$
has $J-2$ singular values equal to $1$ and one equal to $\sqrt{J}$, so
$\kappa(\mathbf{A}_{r})=\sqrt{J}$. The stretched direction is
$\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{e}_{r}$, the log-abundance of the
reference against all other types. Since
$\mathbf{H}_{\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\mathrm{alr}}}=\mathbf{A}_{r}^{-\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{H}_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}\mathbf{A}_{r}^{-1}$,

$$
\frac{\kappa(\mathbf{H}_{\boldsymbol{\rho}})}{J}
\le
\kappa(\mathbf{H}_{\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\mathrm{alr}}})
\le
J\,\kappa(\mathbf{H}_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}),
$$ {#eq-alr-conditioning}

and the curvature along the reference's own direction is divided by
$J$.
:::

*Proof sketch.* (i) is a similarity by an orthogonal matrix. For (ii),
the rows of $\mathbf{D}_{r}$ are $\boldsymbol{e}_{j}-\boldsymbol{e}_{r}$, so
$\mathbf{D}_{r}\mathbf{D}_{r}^{\mathsf{T}}=\mathbf{I}_{J-1}+\mathbf{1}_{J-1}\mathbf{1}_{J-1}^{\mathsf{T}}$,
with eigenvalues $1$ (multiplicity $J-2$) and $J$. Because
$\mathbf{D}_{r}\mathbf{1}_{J}=\boldsymbol{0}$ and $\mathbf{V}$ is an
orthonormal basis of $\mathbf{1}_{J}^{\perp}$, $\mathbf{A}_{r}$ has the
same singular values as $\mathbf{D}_{r}$. The right singular vector for
$\sqrt{J}$ is proportional to
$\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{D}_{r}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{1}_{J-1}
=\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}(\mathbf{1}_{J}-J\boldsymbol{e}_{r})
=-J\,\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{e}_{r}$. The bounds follow from
$\kappa(\mathbf{A}^{-\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{A}^{-1})
\le\kappa(\mathbf{A})^{2}\kappa(\mathbf{H})$ applied in both directions.
$\square$

The constant $\kappa(\mathbf{A}_{r})=\sqrt{J}$ does not depend on $r$,
but the direction it distorts does, so the condition number of the ALR
Hessian depends on the reference. Even a perfectly conditioned problem,
$\mathbf{H}_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}=-\mathbf{I}$, has
$\kappa(\mathbf{H}_{\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\mathrm{alr}}})=J$ in ALR coordinates. For an
illustrative random negative-definite Hessian with $J=6$ (not a DeCovarT
fit), $\kappa=171$ in every orthonormal basis, but between $164$ and
$420$ across the six ALR references. A rare cell type, or one whose
signature is nearly collinear with others, already has weak curvature
along its own direction; choosing it as the ALR reference divides that
curvature by $J$ and makes the problem harder.

These differences affect the solver, not the target:

| Solver ingredient | ILR basis change ($Q$ orthogonal) | ALR reference change ($\mathbf{A}$ oblique) |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Maximiser $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$, $\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}})$, delta-method $\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}})$ | invariant | invariant |
| Pure Newton step | invariant | invariant |
| Gradient norm, steepest-ascent and BFGS steps from an identity start | invariant | changed |
| Spherical trust region, isotropic damping $\mathbf{H}-\mu\mathbf{I}$ | invariant | changed |
| Hessian condition number, accuracy of $\mathcal{I}^{-1}$ | invariant | changed by a factor up to $J$ |

: Which parts of the optimisation depend on the chart convention. {#tbl-chart-invariance}

The default solver is Newton--Raphson on $\boldsymbol{\rho}$
([`deconvolute_ratios_Newton_Raphson()`](../reference/deconvolute_ratios_Marquardt_Levenberg.html)),
a second-order ascent that uses the analytic ILR score and Hessian of
@thm-chain-rule. Its pure Newton direction is the same in every chart;
its safeguards, a spherical trust region and Euclidean step-length
tolerances in `stats::nlminb()`, are unchanged by a rotation of the ILR
basis but not by a change of ALR reference.

::: {#nte-ilr-vs-alr .callout-note}
## Decision: DeCovarT optimises in ILR coordinates

ILR is the only chart of the four that is minimal ($J-1$ free
coordinates), free of a privileged cell type and isometric for the
Aitchison geometry. A change of its convention, the order of cell types
or a different balance basis, is an orthogonal rotation, which leaves
gradient norms and Hessian condition numbers unchanged. A change of ALR
reference is an oblique map whose effect on conditioning depends on the
reference. The solvers, `vcov.decovart_fit()` and the boundary
diagnostics therefore work in ILR coordinates. ALR is kept for
comparison with multinomial-logit models, which use a reference
category.
:::

## Side-by-side comparison of the four charts {#sec-chart-comparison}

| Property | Softmax | ALR | CLR | ILR |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Coordinates | $\boldsymbol{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{J}$ | $\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\mathrm{alr}}=\mathbf{D}_{r}\log\boldsymbol{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{J-1}$ | $\boldsymbol{\xi}=\mathbf{H}_{J}\log\boldsymbol{p}$, with $\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\xi}=0$ | $\boldsymbol{\rho}=\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\log\boldsymbol{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{J-1}$ |
| Inverse map | $\operatorname{softmax}(\boldsymbol{z})$ | $\operatorname{softmax}(\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\mathrm{alr}},0)$ | $\operatorname{softmax}(\boldsymbol{\xi})$ | $\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\rho})$ |
| Feasible after inverse map | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Free and minimal ($J-1$ coordinates) | no: one redundant direction | yes | no: $J$ coordinates on a hyperplane | yes |
| Jacobian of the inverse map | rank $J-1$ out of $J$ | full rank | full rank on $\mathbf{1}^{\perp}$ only | full rank |
| Privileged cell type | none | the reference $r$ | none | none (order fixes the balances) |
| Isometry with Aitchison geometry | no | no (oblique basis) | yes | yes |
| Change of convention | not applicable | oblique, $\kappa(\mathbf{A}_{r})=\sqrt{J}$ | not applicable | orthogonal rotation |
| Hessian conditioning across conventions | singular | depends on the reference | singular | invariant |
| Exact zeros at finite coordinates | no | no | no | no |
| Reading of a coordinate | none (shift-invariant) | log-ratio to the reference | log-ratio to the geometric mean | balance between groups |
| Typical use | neural networks, mixture weights | reference-category regression | exploration, visualisation | likelihood inference, optimisation |

: Four charts for the unit-simplex constraint. {#tbl-chart-comparison}

All four charts guarantee feasibility, and none reaches a face of the
simplex at finite coordinates. For likelihood inference ILR is usually
the best suited: it is the only chart that is at once minimal,
symmetric in the cell types and isometric, which is why Egozcue et al.
introduced it to avoid the drawbacks of both ALR and CLR
[@egozcueIsometricLogratioTransformations2003; @CoordinateRepresentation2015, p. 33]. Its cost is interpretation: a balance is less direct than
a ratio to one reference, and the Helmert balances depend on the order
of cell types unless a partition with a biological meaning is chosen.

## Efficient derivatives of $\boldsymbol{\psi}$ {#sec-ilr-deriv}

Write
$\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{p})
-\boldsymbol{p}\boldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}}$. The Jacobian is

$$
\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}(\boldsymbol{\rho})
=
\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{p}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\mathsf{T}}}
=
\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})\mathbf{V}.
$$ {#eq-ilr-jac}

[`jacobian_isometric_logistic()`](../reference/jacobian_isometric_logistic.html)
returns this $J\times(J-1)$ matrix. Let
$\bar{\boldsymbol{v}}=\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{p}$,
$\boldsymbol{h}_{j}=\mathbf{V}_{j\cdot}-\bar{\boldsymbol{v}}$ and
$\mathbf{C}_{V}=\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})
\mathbf{V}$. Slice $j$ of the map Hessian is

$$
\mathbf{H}_{\psi_{j}}
=
p_{j}\bigl(
  \boldsymbol{h}_{j}\boldsymbol{h}_{j}^{\mathsf{T}}
  -\mathbf{C}_{V}
\bigr).
$$ {#eq-ilr-hess}

[`hessian_isometric_logistic()`](../reference/hessian_isometric_logistic.html)
stores the tensor of shape $(J-1)\times(J-1)\times J$.

## Change of variables: ambient $\boldsymbol{p}$ to ILR $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ {#sec-chain-rule}

Let $\ell_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(\boldsymbol{\rho})
=\ell_{\boldsymbol{y}\mid\boldsymbol{\zeta}}
\bigl(\boldsymbol{\psi}(\boldsymbol{\rho})\bigr)$. The chain rule maps the
unconstrained derivatives of @sec-unconstrained into free Euclidean
coordinates.

::: {#thm-chain-rule}
## Constrained score and Hessian

$$
\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}\ell
=
\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}^{\mathsf{T}}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{p}}\ell
=
\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})\nabla_{\boldsymbol{p}}\ell,
$$ {#eq-chain-first}

$$
\mathbf{H}_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}
=
\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}^{\mathsf{T}}
\mathbf{H}_{\boldsymbol{p}}
\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}
+
\sum_{j=1}^{J}
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial p_{j}}
\mathbf{H}_{\psi_{j}}.
$$ {#eq-chain-second}
:::

::: {#nte-chain-impl .callout-important}
## Implementation map

| Object | Package function |
|:--|:--|
| Ambient score / Hessian | `gradient_loglik_unconstrained()`, `hessian_loglik_unconstrained()` |
| Map Jacobian / Hessian | `jacobian_isometric_logistic()`, `hessian_isometric_logistic()` |
| ILR score / Hessian | `gradient_loglik_constrained()`, `hessian_loglik_constrained()` |

@eq-chain-second is the sum of a covariant pull-back of $\mathbf{H}$ and
a contraction of the ambient score against the map Hessian. Omitting the
second summand is a common bug when porting first-order code to Newton
methods.
:::

## Lagrangian, KKT conditions and what the ILR chart removes {#sec-kkt}

Without a chart, the estimation problem is

$$
\max_{\boldsymbol{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{J}}\ \ell(\boldsymbol{p})
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\mathbf{1}_{J}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{p}=1,
\qquad
\boldsymbol{p}\ge\boldsymbol{0},
$$

with Lagrangian

$$
\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{p},\lambda,\boldsymbol{\nu})
=
\ell(\boldsymbol{p})
-\lambda\bigl(\mathbf{1}_{J}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{p}-1\bigr)
+\boldsymbol{\nu}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{p}.
$$ {#eq-lagrangian}

The constraints are linear, so a constraint qualification holds and
every local maximiser satisfies the KKT conditions
[@boydConvexOptimization2004, sec. 5.5.3]:

$$
\nabla_{\boldsymbol{p}}\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}})
-\lambda\mathbf{1}_{J}
+\boldsymbol{\nu}
=\boldsymbol{0},
\qquad
\mathbf{1}_{J}^{\mathsf{T}}\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}=1,
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\nu}\ge\boldsymbol{0},
\qquad
\nu_{j}\hat{p}_{j}=0.
$$ {#eq-kkt}

- *Interior point* ($\hat{p}_{j}>0$ for all $j$): complementary
  slackness gives $\boldsymbol{\nu}=\boldsymbol{0}$, hence
  $\partial\ell/\partial p_{j}=\lambda$ for every $j$. Every cell type
  has the same marginal gain, so moving mass from one type to another
  does not change $\ell$ to first order. Multiplying by
  $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}^{\mathsf{T}}$ gives the multiplier,
  $\lambda=\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}^{\mathsf{T}}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{p}}\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}})$.
- *Boundary point* ($\hat{p}_{j}=0$): $\partial\ell/\partial p_{j}
  =\lambda-\nu_{j}\le\lambda$. Adding some of type $j$ would not
  increase the likelihood.

**The chart removes the multiplier.** Because
$\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})\mathbf{1}_{J}=\boldsymbol{p}-\boldsymbol{p}(\mathbf{1}_{J}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{p})=\boldsymbol{0}$,
the ILR score of @eq-chain-first ignores any multiple of $\mathbf{1}_{J}$
added to the ambient score:

$$
\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}\ell
=
\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})
\bigl(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{p}}\ell-c\,\mathbf{1}_{J}\bigr)
\quad\text{for every }c,
\qquad
\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})\nabla_{\boldsymbol{p}}\ell
=
\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{p})
\bigl(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{p}}\ell-\lambda(\boldsymbol{p})\mathbf{1}_{J}\bigr),
$$ {#eq-ilr-score-kkt}

with $\lambda(\boldsymbol{p})=\boldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{p}}\ell$.
The ILR score is therefore the KKT stationarity residual of
@eq-kkt, weighted by $\boldsymbol{p}$, with the multiplier set to its
current value. The vector $\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})\nabla_{\boldsymbol{p}}\ell$
lies in $\mathbf{1}_{J}^{\perp}$, on which $\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}$ is an
isometry, so

$$
\bigl\lVert\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}\ell\bigr\rVert
=
\bigl\lVert\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})\nabla_{\boldsymbol{p}}\ell\bigr\rVert,
\qquad
\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}\ell=\boldsymbol{0}
\iff
\nabla_{\boldsymbol{p}}\ell=\lambda\mathbf{1}_{J}.
$$

Stationary points in $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ are exactly the interior KKT
points, the multiplier is recovered afterwards as
$\hat{\lambda}=\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}^{\mathsf{T}}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{p}}\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}})$,
and the score norm that `boundary_diagnostics()` reports does not depend
on the basis. Under ALR the same equivalence holds, but the score norm
changes with the reference.

**Second order: the Hessian of the Lagrangian.** Since
$\sum_{j}\psi_{j}(\boldsymbol{\rho})=1$ for every $\boldsymbol{\rho}$,
$\sum_{j}\mathbf{H}_{\psi_{j}}=\mathbf{0}$, and the curvature term of
@eq-chain-second also ignores the multiplier:

$$
\sum_{j=1}^{J}\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial p_{j}}\mathbf{H}_{\psi_{j}}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{J}\Bigl(\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial p_{j}}-\lambda\Bigr)
\mathbf{H}_{\psi_{j}}.
$$

At an interior KKT point every bracket vanishes, so

$$
\mathbf{H}_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}
=
\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}^{\mathsf{T}}
\nabla^{2}_{\boldsymbol{p}\boldsymbol{p}}\mathcal{L}\,
\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}},
\qquad
\nabla^{2}_{\boldsymbol{p}\boldsymbol{p}}\mathcal{L}=\mathbf{H}_{\boldsymbol{p}},
$$ {#eq-reduced-hessian}

because linear constraints add no curvature to the Lagrangian. The
columns of $\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}=\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})\mathbf{V}$
span $\mathbf{1}_{J}^{\perp}$, the directions $\boldsymbol{d}$ with
$\mathbf{1}_{J}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{d}=0$ that keep the sum equal to
one. @eq-reduced-hessian is thus the Hessian of the Lagrangian reduced
to the tangent space of the constraint, and
$\mathbf{H}_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}\prec 0$ is the classical second-order
sufficient condition
$\boldsymbol{d}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{H}_{\boldsymbol{p}}\boldsymbol{d}<0$
for all $\boldsymbol{d}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ with
$\mathbf{1}_{J}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{d}=0$. Away from stationarity
the curvature term must be kept: it is the price of a curved chart.

**What the chart cannot do.** For finite $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ every
$p_{j}$ is strictly positive, so the inequality multipliers
$\boldsymbol{\nu}$ never become active. A maximiser on a face of the
simplex lies at infinity in $\boldsymbol{\rho}$: the iterates drift,
$\lVert\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}\ell\rVert$ decays only through the
factor $\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{p})$ in @eq-ilr-score-kkt, and
the Hessian becomes singular. The boundary is handled separately
(@sec-structural-zeros). The benchmark reports the projected-gradient
residual
$\lVert\Pi_{\Delta}(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}+\nabla_{\boldsymbol{p}}\ell)-\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}\rVert$,
which is zero exactly at a KKT point, interior or not.

## Perspectives: Bayesian charts and the simplex boundary {#sec-structural-zeros}

::: {#nte-perspectives-charts .callout-note}
## Going further: priors on log-ratio coordinates and estimates on a face

**What DeCovarT does today.** No chart above represents an exact zero at
finite coordinates, because each contains a logarithm. For a true
simplex face the package does **not** send $\log 0$ through the chart: it
fixes the inactive set, optimises ILR coordinates on the remaining
active face
([`restricted_mle_decovart()`](../reference/restricted_mle_decovart.html)),
and checks the KKT inequalities $\partial\ell/\partial p_{j}\le\lambda$
of @sec-kkt for the zero coordinates
([`boundary_diagnostics()`](../reference/boundary_diagnostics.html);
see also the MLE-properties vignette).

**Bayesian versions of the same charts.** A log-ratio chart turns a
prior on the simplex into a prior on Euclidean coordinates, and the
Gaussian bulk likelihood then combines with standard tools
[@pawlowsky-glahnCompositionalDataAnalysis2011].

- *Logistic-normal prior.* A Gaussian prior
  $\boldsymbol{\rho}\sim\mathcal{N}_{J-1}(\boldsymbol{m},\boldsymbol{\Lambda})$
  is a logistic-normal law on $\boldsymbol{p}$. Its log-density adds a
  quadratic penalty to $\ell(\boldsymbol{\rho})$, so the posterior mode
  is a ridge-penalised Newton problem in the same coordinates.
- *Dirichlet prior.* The density of $\boldsymbol{p}$ written in ILR
  coordinates gains the Jacobian factor
  $\lvert\det\partial(p_{1},\ldots,p_{J-1})/\partial\boldsymbol{\rho}\rvert
  =\sqrt{J}\prod_{j}p_{j}$. A Dirichlet$(\boldsymbol{\alpha})$ prior
  therefore becomes $\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}\log p_{j}$ in
  $\boldsymbol{\rho}$, a concave function that pushes the mode away from
  the boundary. Even the uniform prior ($\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\mathbf{1}$)
  is not flat in $\boldsymbol{\rho}$, so a posterior mode depends on the
  chart in which it is computed; posterior means and intervals for
  $\boldsymbol{p}$ do not.
- *CLR or ILR regression.* Covariates enter linearly on the log-ratio
  scale, $\boldsymbol{\rho}_{i}=\mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{z}_{i}+\boldsymbol{u}_{i}$,
  which is the compositional analogue of a multinomial-logit model and
  gives the marginal effect of a covariate on the composition.
- The experimental MAP `CTS` path
  (`scripts/experimental/03_04_DeCovarT_estimate_CTS_MAP_Bayesian.R`,
  derived in the
  [perspectives](theory-decovart-bayesian-wiener.html#sec-map-blup)
  vignette) is one starting point.

**Estimates on the boundary.** Several routes go beyond the active-set
approach; none is implemented.

- *Projection methods* work in $\boldsymbol{p}$ itself: a projected
  Newton or projected-gradient step onto $\Delta^{J-1}$ reaches a face in
  finitely many iterations, and its residual is the KKT residual the
  benchmark already reports.
- *Spike-and-slab or hurdle priors* put positive mass on $p_{j}=0$, so
  the posterior probability that a cell type is absent becomes an
  output, alongside the boundary likelihood-ratio tests of the
  MLE-properties vignette.
- *Charts without a logarithm* reach the boundary at finite coordinates,
  for instance the folded $\alpha$-transformation
  [@tsagrisFoldedModelCompositional2020] or nonparametric regressions
  that admit exact zeros [@tsagrisFlexibleNonparametricRegression2023].
  They are data-side constructions and lose the isometry of ILR.

Rounded zeros (detection limits) remain an imputation problem. True
structural zeros belong on a face and should be fitted as an active-set
or KKT problem, not by substituting a small positive constant into
@eq-ilr-maps.
:::

# Expected Fisher information and Wald inference {#sec-fisher-wald}

Point estimation alone does not report uncertainty. Under a regular
large-sample regime the MLE is asymptotically normal with covariance
given by the inverse Fisher information. DeCovarT builds Wald standard
errors from the *expected* Fisher information of the multivariate-normal
convolution, then maps that information through the ILR chart.

## Unconstrained expected Fisher information {#sec-fisher-p}

For
$\boldsymbol{y}\sim\mathcal{N}_{G}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p},
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})\bigr)$ the expected Fisher information
has entries

$$
I(\boldsymbol{p})_{j\ell}
=
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}^{\top}
\boldsymbol{\Omega}(\boldsymbol{p})
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot \ell}
+
2p_{j}p_{\ell}\,
\mathrm{tr}\bigl(
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}(\boldsymbol{p})\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}(\boldsymbol{p})\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell}
\bigr).
$$ {#eq-fisher-p}

The first summand is the mean contribution (a $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$-inner
product of signature columns); the second is the covariance contribution
of the quadratic map
$\boldsymbol{p}\mapsto\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})$. See the
multivariate-normal formula on
[Wikipedia: Fisher information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_information#Multivariate_normal_distribution).
[`expected_fisher_unconstrained()`](../reference/expected_fisher_unconstrained.html)
implements @eq-fisher-p.

::: {#nte-obs-vs-exp .callout-note}
## Observed versus expected information

The analytic Hessian of @sec-unconstrained is the *observed* information
(up to sign). Wald intervals in `decovart_fit` use the *expected*
information @eq-fisher-p, which does not depend on the residual
$\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}$ and is positive definite under
the usual full-rank assumptions on $(\boldsymbol{\mu},\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}\})$.

The two are consistent by construction. Substituting
$\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{r}]=\boldsymbol{0}$ and
$\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{r}\boldsymbol{r}^{\top}]
=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})$ into @eq-hess-diag and
@eq-hess-off cancels the determinant traces against the residual traces
and returns @eq-fisher-p exactly, i.e.
$\mathbb{E}[-\mathbf{H}]=I(\boldsymbol{p})$. That identity only holds with
the factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ of @nte-halfdet in place.
:::

## Constrained case: ILR delta method {#sec-fisher-rho}

Fisher information transforms as a covariant quadratic form under the
ILR chart. With
$\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}
=\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})\mathbf{V}$,

$$
I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}
=
\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}^{\mathsf{T}}
I(\boldsymbol{p})
\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}
=
\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}
\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})
I(\boldsymbol{p})
\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})
\mathbf{V}.
$$ {#eq-fisher-rho}

The mean/covariance split of @eq-fisher-p pulls back separately,
$I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}=I_{\boldsymbol{\rho},\mathrm{mean}}
+I_{\boldsymbol{\rho},\mathrm{cov}}$. Under regularity,
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}
\overset{a}{\sim}
\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\rho}_{0},I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}^{-1})$
[@vaartAsymptoticStatistics2000].
The first-order delta method [@oehlertNoteDeltaMethod1992] then returns
the simplex covariance used by
[`vcov.decovart_fit()`](../reference/fit_decovart.html),

$$
\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}})
\approx
\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}
I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}^{-1}
\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}^{\mathsf{T}}.
$$ {#eq-delta-p}

Diagonal square roots are asymptotic standard errors; Wald intervals at
level $1-\alpha$ are
$\hat{p}_{j}\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\mathrm{SE}_{j}$ with
$z_{q}=\Phi^{-1}(q)$, as in
[`confint.decovart_fit()`](../reference/fit_decovart.html).
[`vcov_ilr_delta()`](../reference/vcov_ilr_delta.html) implements
@eq-fisher-rho--@eq-delta-p. Orthogonal rotations of $\mathbf{V}$ leave
@eq-delta-p unchanged. The construction is undefined on the simplex
boundary (the log-ratio chart blows up); the helper then returns `NA`
with a warning.

::: {#nte-wald-limits .callout-warning}
## Wald is the cheapest, not the safest, interval

@eq-delta-p linearises the ILR chart at $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$, so it is
neither invariant to a non-orthogonal reparametrisation nor confined to
$[0,1]$, and it degenerates entirely when a proportion reaches a simplex
face. The companion vignette
[MLE properties and asymptotic inference](theory-DeCovarT-MLE-properties.html)
derives the alternatives: profile likelihood-ratio intervals, the
chi-bar-square calibration of Chernoff and of Self and Liang for nulls on
the boundary, a parametric bootstrap, and a reference-sample bootstrap
of donors or cells (or a Dirichlet composition sweep). It also shows why
these limits need replicate samples that share one composition.
Shuffling genes or cell-type names of an averaged signature is not a
bootstrap: the maximised likelihood is equivariant under relabelling.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Numerical speed-ups and solver safeguards {#sec-numerical-speedups}

The analytic maps above are only half of a usable optimiser. Practical
bottlenecks that showed up on the hybrid scenario in
[Covariance-driven hybrid scenario](fig03-covariance-driven.html#sec-hybrid-deconvolution)
live in `R/02_03_decovart_estimate_ratios.R`.

---

### Cache a Cholesky factorisation of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})$

Within one iteration, objective / gradient / Hessian callbacks hit the
same trial $\boldsymbol{p}$. The helper `.sigma_p_factorisation()` caches
a single Cholesky factor
$\boldsymbol{R}$ with
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})=\boldsymbol{R}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{R}$
and returns
$\log\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})=2\sum_g\log R_{gg}$
together with the precision
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}(\boldsymbol{p})=\boldsymbol{R}^{-1}\boldsymbol{R}^{-\mathsf{T}}$
(via `chol2inv`) without repeating an $O(G^{3})$ factorisation.

[`loglik_multivariate()`](../reference/loglik_multivariate.html) then
evaluates the Mahalanobis term exactly as `mvtnorm::dmvnorm`
[@R-mvtnorm]: it solves $\boldsymbol{R}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{z}
=\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}$ by
`backsolve(..., transpose = TRUE)` and takes
$\lVert\boldsymbol{z}\rVert^{2}$, rather than forming
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}(\boldsymbol{p})$ and a dense quadratic form. The two
routes agree to machine precision; the backsolve path is the one used
for the objective, while the cached inverse is retained for the analytic
score and Hessian, which need
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}(\boldsymbol{p})$ in several trace and inner-product
terms. A QR factorisation of the covariance itself would recover the
same log-determinant and quadratic form at a larger $O(G^{3})$ constant
and is not used: Cholesky is the natural factorisation of a symmetric
positive-definite matrix.

The implemented log-density omits the additive
$-\tfrac{G}{2}\log(2\pi)$ of the full Gaussian, which does not depend
on $\boldsymbol{p}$ and therefore cannot change the MLE, the score, or
the Hessian. Tests check that subtracting that constant recovers
`dmvnorm(..., log = TRUE)` exactly.

---

### Guard the box-constrained L-BFGS-B path

`deconvolute_ratios_L_BFGS_B()` optimises in $\boldsymbol{p}$ with boxes
$[0,1]^{J}$ that do not enforce $\mathbf{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}=1$. Near
$\sum_{j}p_{j}\approx 0$ (or on a failed `chol()`), safeguarded wrappers
return a finite penalty and a zero gradient rather than aborting
`optim()`.

---

### `marqLevAlg` Hessian sign under `minimize = FALSE`

The optional Marquardt–Levenberg solver
(`fit_decovart(method = "Marquardt-Levenberg")`) calls
[`marqLevAlg`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=marqLevAlg)
[@R-marqLevAlg], which implements Marquardt–Levenberg with the
relative-distance-to-minimum (RDM) rule of Commenges et al.
[@commengesNewtonLikeAlgorithmLikelihood2006]. With
`minimize = FALSE`, the package negates only `fn` and `gr`; the analytic
`hess` is passed through unchanged while internal Cholesky routines
assume a **positive-definite** matrix at the optimum. When maximising a
log-likelihood, pass
`hess = function(...) -hessian_loglik_constrained(...)`. Reported
upstream as
[VivianePhilipps/marqLevAlgParallel#3](https://github.com/VivianePhilipps/marqLevAlgParallel/issues/3).
:::

# Model objects and S3 accessors {#sec-s3}

[`fit_decovart()`](../reference/fit_decovart.html) returns a `decovart_fit`
object with standard S3 methods for coefficients, fitted values, residuals,
and (under regularity) a delta-method covariance. The chunk below mirrors
the appendix equivariance setup:

```{r}
#| label: s3-accessors
#| warning: false
library(DeCovarT)
genes <- paste0("g", 1:3)
cts <- paste0("ct", 1:2)
mu <- matrix(
  c(20, 40, 25, 35, 30, 22),
  nrow = 3,
  dimnames = list(genes, cts)
)
Sigma <- array(0, dim = c(3, 3, 2), dimnames = list(genes, genes, cts))
Sigma[, , 1] <- diag(c(1.0, 1.2, 0.8))
Sigma[, , 2] <- diag(c(1.5, 0.9, 1.1))
p_true <- c(0.65, 0.35)
y <- matrix(
  drop(mu %*% p_true + rnorm(3, sd = 0.05)),
  ncol = 1L,
  dimnames = list(genes, "s1")
)

fit <- fit_decovart(
  mu,
  y,
  Sigma = Sigma,
  itmax = 80
)
coef(fit)
nobs(fit)
c(
  n_genes = attr(nobs(fit), "n_genes"),
  n_celltypes = attr(nobs(fit), "n_celltypes")
)
fitted(fit)
residuals(fit)
vcov(fit)
```

`formula()` and `predict()` are not implemented: DeCovarT does not
forecast bulk expression.

# Numerical consistency of the likelihood and its derivatives {#sec-numerical-consistency}

Analytic formulae can be differentiated correctly *and* still implement
the wrong objective. The checks below separate those two questions.
They are the same identities that
`tests/testthat/test-02_03_decovart_estimate_ratios.R` and
`tests/testthat/test-03_01_decovart_inference.R` enforce on every
package build; the chunks here are a readable, small-\(G\) illustration.

```{r}
#| label: consistency-setup
#| include: false
library(DeCovarT)
genes <- paste0("g", 1:3)
cts <- paste0("ct", 1:3)
mu_chk <- matrix(
  c(20, 40, 15, 40, 20, 25, 25, 30, 35),
  nrow = 3,
  dimnames = list(genes, cts)
)
Sigma_chk <- array(0, dim = c(3, 3, 3), dimnames = list(genes, genes, cts))
Sigma_chk[, , 1] <- diag(c(1, 1.5, 1.2))
Sigma_chk[, , 2] <- diag(c(1.1, 0.9, 1.3))
Sigma_chk[, , 3] <- diag(c(0.8, 1.2, 1.0))
p_chk <- c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2)
set.seed(1)
y_chk <- drop(mu_chk %*% p_chk) + c(0.4, -0.2, 0.1)
cov_chk <- .compute_global_variance(p_chk, Sigma_chk)
```

## Density against `mvtnorm`

The first check is against an independent implementation of the
multivariate Gaussian log-density, not against our own inverse. With
the $\tfrac{1}{2}\log\det$ factor restored, DeCovarT and
`mvtnorm::dmvnorm` [@R-mvtnorm] differ by exactly
$\tfrac{G}{2}\log(2\pi)$ (DeCovarT omits the negative constant):

```{r}
#| label: consistency-dmvnorm
n_genes <- length(y_chk)
ours <- loglik_multivariate(p_chk, y_chk, mu_chk, Sigma_chk)
reference <- if (requireNamespace("mvtnorm", quietly = TRUE)) {
  as.numeric(mvtnorm::dmvnorm(
    y_chk,
    mean = drop(mu_chk %*% p_chk),
    sigma = cov_chk,
    log = TRUE
  ))
} else {
  residual <- y_chk - drop(mu_chk %*% p_chk)
  as.numeric(
    -0.5 * determinant(cov_chk, logarithm = TRUE)$modulus -
      0.5 * drop(crossprod(residual, solve(cov_chk, residual))) -
      0.5 * n_genes * log(2 * pi)
  )
}
c(
  loglik_multivariate = ours,
  dmvnorm = reference,
  difference = ours - 0.5 * n_genes * log(2 * pi) - reference
)
```

A finite-difference check of the *same* objective cannot detect a shared
factor-of-two error in the log-likelihood and its derivatives. That is
why this density comparison is independent of `numDeriv`.

## Richardson extrapolation of the score and Hessian

Once the objective is the intended Gaussian, the analytic score and
Hessian are checked against Richardson extrapolation in `numDeriv`
[@R-numDeriv]. Richardson's tableau extrapolates central differences to
cancel successive even powers of the step size, which is more accurate
than a single two-point stencil at the same $O(\varepsilon^{-1})$ cost
in function evaluations.

```{r}
#| label: consistency-numderiv
if (!requireNamespace("numDeriv", quietly = TRUE)) {
  numderiv_report <- c(gradient_rel = NA_real_, hessian_rel = NA_real_)
} else {
  grad_n <- numDeriv::grad(
    loglik_multivariate,
    p_chk,
    method = "Richardson",
    method.args = list(eps = 1e-4, r = 6),
    y = y_chk,
    mean_signature_matrix = mu_chk,
    Sigma = Sigma_chk
  )
  hess_n <- numDeriv::hessian(
    loglik_multivariate,
    p_chk,
    method = "Richardson",
    method.args = list(eps = 1e-4, r = 4),
    y = y_chk,
    mean_signature_matrix = mu_chk,
    Sigma = Sigma_chk
  )
  grad_a <- gradient_loglik_unconstrained(
    p_chk, y_chk, mu_chk, Sigma_chk
  )
  hess_a <- hessian_loglik_unconstrained(
    p_chk, y_chk, mu_chk, Sigma_chk
  )
  numderiv_report <- c(
    gradient_rel = max(abs(grad_a - grad_n)) / max(abs(grad_n)),
    hessian_rel = max(abs(hess_a - hess_n)) / max(abs(hess_n))
  )
}
numderiv_report
```

Relative discrepancies of order \(10^{-8}\) are typical on this
three-gene toy; that is the same tolerance used in the test suite.

## Expected information versus Monte Carlo \(\mathbb{E}[-\mathbf{H}]\)

Matching `numDeriv` shows that the derivatives belong to the implemented
objective. Matching the *expected* Fisher information
[@eq-fisher-p] to a Monte Carlo average of \(-\mathbf{H}(\boldsymbol{p};
\boldsymbol{Y})\) shows that the objective is the Gaussian whose
information matrix we use for Wald intervals. Draw
\(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(b)}\sim\mathcal{N}_G(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p},
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p}))\) at the *true* \(\boldsymbol{p}\)
(the parametric bootstrap of
[`bootstrap_decovart()`](../reference/bootstrap_decovart.html), used here
as a diagnostic rather than as an inferential procedure):

```{r}
#| label: consistency-fisher-mc
set.seed(2)
n_mc <- 40L
info <- expected_fisher_unconstrained(p_chk, mu_chk, Sigma_chk)
neg_hess <- array(NA_real_, c(3L, 3L, n_mc))
for (b in seq_len(n_mc)) {
  y_b <- MASS::mvrnorm(
    n = 1L,
    mu = drop(mu_chk %*% p_chk),
    Sigma = cov_chk
  )
  neg_hess[, , b] <- -hessian_loglik_unconstrained(
    p_chk, y_b, mu_chk, Sigma_chk
  )
}
mc_info <- apply(neg_hess, c(1L, 2L), mean)
c(
  rel_frobenius = sqrt(sum((mc_info - info)^2)) / sqrt(sum(info^2))
)
```

The same identity is what closed the factor-of-two inconsistency: with
the old \(-\log\det\) objective, \(\mathbb{E}[-\mathbf{H}]\) could not
equal \(I(\boldsymbol{p})\). A few dozen draws already bring the relative
Frobenius gap below \(10^{-2}\) on this toy; the test suite uses a
tighter Monte Carlo.

A related, weaker check compares the empirical covariance of
parametric-bootstrap MLEs to the Cramér–Rao map
[`vcov_ilr_delta()`](../reference/vcov_ilr_delta.html). That comparison
is noisy at small replication (see
[MLE properties](theory-DeCovarT-MLE-properties.html#sec-replication)
for why one bulk column is not an asymptotic sample) and is therefore
left to the inference vignette and to
[`bootstrap_decovart()`](../reference/bootstrap_decovart.html).

# Structure-aware covariance backends {#sec-structure-backends}

Every solver call factorises
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})=\sum_j p_j^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$.
The dense Cholesky in `.sigma_p_factorisation()` is the universal default and
the only method that needs no assumptions. When the covariance inherits
structure from the underlying gene network, the same log-determinant and
solves can be obtained far more cheaply. Exploiting band, sparse and
diagonal-plus-low-rank structure in a Newton-type solver is standard
practice [@boydConvexOptimization2004, §9.7]; the backends below make that
structure explicit for DeCovarT.

[`new_decovart_covariance()`](../reference/new_decovart_covariance.html)
wraps the covariance array with a declared `structure`, and the operators
[`sigma_logdet()`](../reference/sigma_logdet.html),
[`sigma_solve()`](../reference/sigma_solve.html),
[`sigma_quadform()`](../reference/sigma_quadform.html) and
[`sigma_trace_precision_times()`](../reference/sigma_trace_precision_times.html)
return exactly the quantities the objective, score and Hessian need. They
expose *operations*, never a materialised dense precision: a sparse or
Woodbury solve must not be silently undone by a dense `chol2inv`.

## Decision tree {#sec-backend-decision}

Structure is supplied explicitly, never inferred from floating-point
near-zeros, so a numerical near-zero is never mistaken for an exact
conditional independence.
[`covariance_structure_from_graph_model()`](../reference/covariance_structure_from_graph_model.html)
maps a network topology to the recommended backend. A sparse
*precision* $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$ does not imply a sparse *covariance*
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$; only structure that survives in
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})$ itself accelerates the likelihood.

```{.tikz}
%%| label: fig-backend-decision
%%| fig-cap: Choosing a covariance backend; dense Cholesky is the default and structured backends are exact refinements.
%%| filename: fig-backend-decision
%%| alt: Decision tree. The covariance Sigma(p), the sum over j of p_j squared Sigma_j, leads to a question about its declared structure. Five branches: no structure gives dense Cholesky at cost G cubed; disconnected modules give block Cholesky; ordered local dependence gives banded Cholesky; a fixed sparse pattern gives sparse Cholesky with a symbolic ordering computed once; shared programmes or hub genes give a Woodbury or Schur update at cost G r squared.
\begin{tikzpicture}[node distance=7mm]
\node[keybox] (A) {$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})=\sum_{j} p_j^{2}\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$};
\node[choice, below=of A] (B) {Declared covariance\\ structure?};
\node[box, anchor=north, text width=2.8cm] (D) at ($(B.south)+(-7.0,-1.1)$) {\textit{none (default)}\\[3pt] Dense Cholesky\\ $O(G^{3})$};
\node[box, anchor=north, text width=2.8cm] (E) at ($(B.south)+(-3.5,-1.1)$) {\textit{disconnected modules (stochastic block model)}\\[3pt] Block Cholesky\\ $O\bigl(\sum_b G_b^{3}\bigr)$};
\node[box, anchor=north, text width=2.8cm] (F) at ($(B.south)+(0,-1.1)$) {\textit{ordered local dependence (band, AR)}\\[3pt] Banded Cholesky\\ $O(G b^{2})$};
\node[box, anchor=north, text width=2.8cm] (G) at ($(B.south)+(3.5,-1.1)$) {\textit{fixed sparse pattern (Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi, scale-free, small-world)}\\[3pt] Sparse Cholesky,\\ symbolic ordering once};
\node[box, anchor=north, text width=2.8cm] (H) at ($(B.south)+(7.0,-1.1)$) {\textit{shared programmes, bridge hubs (pathways, housekeeping)}\\[3pt] Woodbury / Schur\\ $O(G r^{2})$};
\draw[edge] (A) -- (B);
\foreach \n in {D,E,F,G,H} \draw[edge] (B.south) -- (\n.north);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

Each refinement is exact, not approximate:

- **Block** (disconnected gene modules, e.g. a stochastic block model with no
  between-block edges [@hollandStochasticBlockmodelsFirst1983]).
  $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})$ is block-diagonal, so the
  log-likelihood separates over blocks and one Cholesky per block replaces
  one dense Cholesky.
- **Band / AR.** Only genes within bandwidth $b$ covary; a banded Cholesky
  costs $O(G b^{2})$ [@golubMatrixComputations2013].
- **Sparse** (Erdős–Rényi, scale-free
  [@barabasiEmergenceScalingRandom1999], small-world
  [@wattsCollectiveDynamicsSmallworld1998]). The fill-reducing ordering is
  a *symbolic factorisation* computed once and reused for every numeric
  refactor as $\boldsymbol{p}$ changes; only the numerical Cholesky
  repeats [@chenAlgorithm887CHOLMOD2008].
- **Diagonal + low rank.** Genes interact through $r\ll G$ shared regulatory
  programs, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j=\mathbf{D}_j+\mathbf{U}\mathbf{C}_j
  \mathbf{U}^{\mathsf{T}}$ — the factor-analysis form
  $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\mathsf{T}}+\boldsymbol{\Psi}$.
  The Woodbury identity and the matrix-determinant lemma
  [@hagerUpdatingInverseMatrix1989] move the $O(G^{3})$ cost to the low
  rank $r$. A few bridge / housekeeping hub genes give the arrow-matrix
  special case handled by the same Schur-complement algebra.

```{r}
#| label: backend-usage
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
# Declare structure explicitly, then use the operator interface.
cov <- new_decovart_covariance(Sigma, structure = "diag_lowrank",
  diagonal = D, loadings = U, core = C)
ld <- sigma_logdet(cov, p)            # log det Sigma(p)
z  <- sigma_solve(cov, p, residual)   # Sigma(p)^{-1} r, no dense inverse
q  <- sigma_quadform(cov, p, residual)
```

## Computational complexity {#sec-backend-complexity}

For a dense symmetric positive-definite $G\times G$ matrix the Cholesky
factorisation costs about $G^{3}/3$ flops before the cheaper triangular
solves [@golubMatrixComputations2013]. The structured backends reduce that
leading term:

| Structure | When it applies | Factorisation cost | Backend argument |
|:----------|:----------------|:-------------------|:-----------------|
| Dense | universal default | $O(G^{3})$ | (default) |
| Block | disconnected modules (SBM) | $O(\sum_b G_b^{3})$; $\approx B^{2}$ saving for $B$ equal blocks | `structure = "block"` |
| Band / AR | bandwidth $b$ | $O(G b^{2})$ | `structure = "band"` |
| Sparse | fixed sparse pattern | pattern-dependent; symbolic ordering reused across $\boldsymbol{p}$ | `structure = "sparse"` |
| Diagonal + low rank | $r$ shared programs | $O(G r^{2})$ solve, $O(r^{3})$ core | `structure = "diag_lowrank"` |

: Leading factorisation cost per backend. $G$ genes, $J$ cell types, $B$
blocks of size $G_b$, bandwidth $b$, rank $r\ll G$. {#tbl-backend-complexity}

These are worst-case flop counts and only rough predictors of wall-clock
time on cache-based hardware with tuned BLAS; the block and low-rank savings
($\approx B^{2}$ and $O(G^{2})\!\to\!O(Gr^{2})$ respectively) are the most
robust. The `"band"` and `"sparse"` backends use the imported `Matrix`
package (supernodal sparse Cholesky in CHOLMOD,
[@chenAlgorithm887CHOLMOD2008]).
`scripts/supp_S2_covariance_inversion.R` verifies each backend against
the dense path to machine precision. Approximate sparse Cholesky of
otherwise dense kernel covariances is a separate research line
[@schäferCompressionInversionApproximate2020]; the `"sparse"` backend here
is exact for a declared sparse pattern, not that approximation.
